title: The Wave Nature of Matter Causes Quantization
lead: Bohr had to assume that the angular momentum of an electron in its orbit is quantized. This section asks why, using the wave nature of the electron, and then looks at what becomes of the idea of a well-defined orbit once the electron is treated as a wave.
objectives: Define and describe quantization of angular momentum.
Calculate the angular momentum for an orbit of atom.
Define and describe the wave-like properties of matter.
summary_html:
• Quantization of orbital energy is caused by the wave nature of matter. Allowed orbits in atoms occur for constructive interference of electrons in the orbit, requiring an integral number of wavelengths to fit in an orbit’s circumference; that is, $$n\klamorb = 2\pi\krn\;(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots),$$ where $\klamorb$ is the electron’s de Broglie wavelength.
  • Owing to the wave nature of electrons and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, there are no well-defined orbits; rather, there are clouds of probability.
  • Bohr correctly proposed that the energy and radii of the orbits of electrons in atoms are quantized, with energy for transitions between orbits given by $$\kdE = h\kf = \kEini - \kEfin,$$ where $\kdE$ is the change in energy between the initial and final orbits and $h\kf$ is the energy of an absorbed or emitted photon.
  • It is useful to plot orbit energies on a vertical graph called an energy-level diagram.
  • The allowed orbits are circular, Bohr proposed, and must have quantized orbital angular momentum given by $$\kL = \kme\kv\krn = n\frac{h}{2\pi}\;(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots),$$ where $\kL$ is the angular momentum, $\krn$ is the radius of orbit $n$, and $h$ is Planck’s constant.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 30.44) (a) Waves on a string have a wavelength related to the length of the string, allowing them to interfere constructively. (b) If we imagine the string bent into a closed circle, we get a rough idea of how electrons in circular orbits can interfere constructively. (c) If the wavelength does not fit into the circumference, the electron interferes destructively; it cannot exist in such an orbit. (Figure 30.45) The third and fourth allowed circular orbits have three and four wavelengths, respectively, in their circumferences.

The ground state of a hydrogen atom has a probability cloud describing the position of its electron. The probability of finding the electron is proportional to the darkness of the cloud. The electron can be closer or farther than the Bohr radius, but it is very unlikely to be a great distance from the nucleus.

figure.alt: Two graphs of amplitude against x. Particle X has a long wave packet of many oscillations spread widely about x0, its largest peaks reaching A0. Particle Y has a short, narrow packet bunched closely about x0, with peaks rising well above A0.

exercises.prompt:
This figure shows graphical representations of the wave functions of two particles, X and Y, that are moving in the positive x-direction. The maximum amplitude of particle X’s wave function is A0. Which particle has a greater probability of being located at position x0 at this instant, and why?
  1. Particle X, because the wave function of particle X spends more time passing through x0 than the wave function of particle Y.
  2. Particle X, because the wave function of particle X has a longer wavelength than the wave function of particle Y.
  3. Particle Y, because the wave function of particle Y is narrower than the wave function of particle X.
  4. Particle Y, because the wave function of particle Y has a greater amplitude near x0 than the wave function of particle X.

answer.solution: The chance of finding a particle at a place depends on how large its wave function is there: the greater the amplitude at a point, the more likely a measurement is to find the particle at that point, just as the darkest part of a probability cloud is where the electron is most often found. Compare the two graphs at $x_0$ only. The wave function of particle $Y$ rises well above $A_0$ near $x_0$, while that of particle $X$ reaches at most $A_0$. The width of a packet and its wavelength describe how the wave is spread out and how fast the particle moves, not how likely it is to be at one point, so the reason to look for is the amplitude near $x_0$.

figure.alt: Two graphs of amplitude against x. Particle X has a long wave packet of many oscillations spread widely about x0, its largest peaks reaching A0. Particle Y has a short, narrow packet bunched closely about x0, with peaks rising well above A0.

exercises.prompt: In the figure of the wave functions of particle X and particle Y, explain qualitatively the difference in the wave functions of particle X and particle Y. Which particle is more likely to be found at a larger distance from the coordinate x0 and why? Which particle is more likely be found exactly at x0 and why?

answer.solution: The wave function of particle $X$ is spread over a wide range of $x$ with a modest amplitude, while that of particle $Y$ is bunched into a narrow region about $x_0$ with a large amplitude. Where the wave function is large, the particle is likely to be found. Particle $X$ has a noticeable amplitude far from $x_0$ on either side, so it is the one more likely to be found at a larger distance from $x_0$; its position is less certain. Particle $Y$ has almost no amplitude away from $x_0$ and its largest amplitude right there, so it is more likely to be found exactly at $x_0$. By the uncertainty principle, the narrower packet of $Y$ comes with a larger uncertainty in its momentum, which shows up as the wider range of wavelengths a short packet contains.

exercises.prompt:
For an electron with a de Broglie wavelength λ, which of the following orbital circumferences within the atom would be disallowed? Select two answers.
  1. 0.5 λ
  2. λ
  3. 1.5 λ
  4. 2 λ

answer.solution: An orbit is allowed only where the electron interferes constructively with itself, which needs a whole number of wavelengths to fit round the circumference: $n\klamorb = 2\pi\krn$ with $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$. Check each circumference against that condition. A circumference of one or two wavelengths is a whole number of them, so those orbits are allowed. A circumference of half a wavelength or one and a half wavelengths leaves the wave out of step with itself after one trip round, so it interferes destructively and those two orbits are disallowed.

exercises.prompt: We have discovered that an electron’s orbit must contain an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths. Explain why, under ordinary conditions, this makes it impossible for electrons to spiral in to merge with the positively charged nucleus.

answer.solution: To spiral in, the electron would have to pass through orbits of every smaller radius, but only orbits whose circumference holds a whole number of wavelengths are allowed, and the smallest of them holds just one wavelength, $n = 1$, at the radius $\kaB$. There is no allowed orbit with fewer than one wavelength in its circumference, so there is no allowed state closer to the nucleus. In any orbit between the allowed ones the electron interferes destructively with itself and cannot exist there. The electron in the lowest orbit therefore has nowhere lower to go, and it cannot exist closer to or inside the nucleus; this is why atoms do not collapse and have the sizes they do.

exercises.prompt: How is the de Broglie wavelength of electrons related to the quantization of their orbits in atoms and molecules?

answer.solution: A bound electron behaves as a wave whose wavelength is its de Broglie wavelength, $\klam = h/\kme\kv$. In a circular orbit the wave runs round and meets itself, and it survives only if it interferes constructively, which happens when a whole number of wavelengths fits in the circumference, $n\klamorb = 2\pi\krn$. Only certain orbits meet that condition, so the orbits are quantized. Putting the de Broglie wavelength into the condition gives $\kme\kv\krn = nh/2\pi$, the quantization of angular momentum that Bohr had to assume. In molecules the same idea holds: the allowed states are those whose waves fit the space the electron is confined to.
